claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are governed by the interplay among short-range ordering, dislocation behavior, and grain-boundary interactions.
Electron nanodiffraction and atomistic simulations can elucidate the proposed interplay among short-range ordering, dislocations, and grain boundaries.
Controlled elemental additions and processing changes vary alloy composition and microstructure.
Short-range ordering, dislocation density, and grain-boundary characteristics are structural mediators of hardness and strength.
Interactions among short-range ordering, dislocations, and grain boundaries influence dislocation mobility.
Interactions among short-range ordering, dislocations, and grain boundaries influence the formation of deformation twins.
Changes in dislocation mobility and deformation-twin formation control the mechanical behavior of high-entropy alloys.
Alloys with optimized short-range ordering and grain-boundary interactions will have greater hardness than alloys with random or unoptimized microstructures.
Alloys with optimized short-range ordering and grain-boundary interactions will have greater strength than alloys with random or unoptimized microstructures.
The proposed governing behavior applies at room temperature under quasi-static loading.
The proposed governing behavior may not apply under high-temperature loading.
The proposed governing behavior may not apply under dynamic loading.
A lack of correlation between hardness or strength and short-range ordering or grain-boundary interactions would fail to support the hypothesis.
